verses.translation_literal: A miktam of David. Keep me, O God, for I have taken refuge in you.
verses.translation_dramatic: A miktam, a golden psalm, David's own. He begins low and fast, without ceremony: Keep me, God. There is no more preamble than a man gives who has already run to the only wall he trusts. For in you I have taken refuge, he says. The running is behind him, the shelter is under his hand.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a prayer by a man already inside the shelter. The verb 'chasah' (take refuge) is the word for running under a rock, a wing or a shadow, and the perfect tense says it is done: 'I have taken refuge', not 'I would like to'. Play the opening as a plea from someone who is safe because he has fled to God, not a stranger knocking on the door. 'El' is God as strong one, the generic word for deity; the speaker uses it, not the covenant name, for the opening plea.

The heading is part of the Hebrew verse (the KJV numbers it as 16:0), and it hides a riddle. 'Miktam' is a word nobody can confirm. Rashi offers three guesses: a musical term, 'mach ve-tam', 'humble and whole' (the Talmud's reading, which he admits the verse does not support here), or 'ketem', gold, as in Song 5:11. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion go with gold: a prized, treasured psalm. The Targum goes in another direction, 'a chiselled/engraved [piece]' (גליפא תריצא). The KJV just transliterates 'Michtam'. YLT's 'A Secret Treasure' is a guess. Keep the word unglossed in your mouth.

The KJV 'Preserve me' and 'put my trust' are both a little off: 'shamar' is 'guard, keep watch over', a soldier's word, and 'chasah' is physical shelter (ASV and Rashi's source text get closer with 'take refuge').

philological_notes.note: A heading term of uncertain meaning, found in Psalms 16 and 56-60. Rashi lists three options (a musical term; 'humble and whole'; golden, from 'ketem'); Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion take it as 'precious like gold'; the Targum has 'engraved'.
To take refuge, to shelter under something (a wing, a rock). Perfect tense: the speaker has already done it, and the prayer rests on that. Radak adds 'in you, and not in another'.

verses.translation_literal: You [fem.] have said to YHWH: "My Lord [are] you; my good [is] not upon you."
verses.translation_dramatic: And now the voice turns and speaks to someone near. You have said it to the LORD, you have said it aloud: You are my Lord. Whatever good I hold, I do not hold it over you. It is not a debt you owe.
verses.directors_commentary:
Start with the grammar, because it is the first surprise. 'You said' is feminine singular, and the psalm has so far been a man speaking to God. Nobody agrees who the 'you' is. Rashi gives two readings: David speaking to the congregation of Israel, and, as the other way, David speaking to his own soul (nefesh is feminine in Hebrew). Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David take the soul, and the Targum puts 'my soul' into the text. Malbim hears something quite different: the feminine 'you' is the nation that worships other gods, which concedes that YHWH is God over all and then denies him any part in its daily good. Play it as a man talking himself into what he already knows, or as a man turning to someone beside him.

The last clause has no safe translation. Literally 'my good [is] not upon you.' Rashi, Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David read it as humility: the good you do me is not something you owe me, it is all grace. The ASV and BBE choose 'no good beyond/but you'. The KJV's 'my goodness extendeth not to thee' is stiff and seems to mean that God needs nothing from the speaker. Keep the Hebrew's bareness and let the actor choose.

The KJV adds 'O my soul' and the divine name sits under the title 'the Lord'; here the Hebrew has the name YHWH followed by 'adonay, 'my Lord', and the second word is what the speaker is claiming.

philological_notes.note: Second person feminine singular. The commentators resolve the odd 'you' in different ways: the soul (Radak, Meiri, Ibn Ezra, Metzudat David), the congregation of Israel or the soul (Rashi), the idol-worshipping nation (Malbim).

Literally 'my good [is] not upon you.' The preposition al can mean 'incumbent on' or 'beyond'. Rashi, Radak and Metzudat David read 'not an obligation of yours'; the ASV and BBE read 'nothing good beyond you'. The negative bal is rare and poetic.

verses.translation_literal: To the holy ones who [are] in the land, they, and the majestic ones: all my delight [is] in them.
verses.translation_dramatic: As for the holy ones, the ones who are in the land, here, on this ground, the noble ones, the great ones: all my delight is in them.
verses.directors_commentary:
This verse is a broken sentence, and the break is the point. It starts with a bare 'to the holy ones' with no verb, adds a flat 'they', and then a second group, the majestic, before it finally gets to 'all my delight'. Do not smooth it. The KJV smooths it with 'But', which makes it a contrast to the previous verse that the Hebrew does not state, and the ASV and BBE turn the whole thing into a calm sentence, 'they are the excellent'.

Who are the holy ones 'in the land'? The tradition pulls three ways. Rashi and Meiri hear the dead: Rashi's 'holy ones buried in the earth who walked before you in truth', Meiri the patriarchs, who are the reason God does good to the speaker. Radak and Metzudat David hear the living pious, to be respected and learned from. Malbim hears gods: the idols whom the nation counts as the sources of its good. Ibn Ezra explicitly refuses the patriarchs; he says that explaining it that way does not suit the sense of the psalm. For him the holy ones are people on earth, and 'in the land' is added because 'holy ones' normally means angels, so the phrase marks these as the earthly ones. Direct the line as admiration, with a gesture at the ground.

The KJV's 'saints' carries later church sense; qedoshim here simply means those set apart. 'Excellent' for 'adirim' loses the sense of grandeur and weight; this is the word used of mighty waters and noble men.

philological_notes.note: 'Holy ones', those set apart. Ibn Ezra stresses that the word usually means angels, which is why the psalm adds 'who are in the land'; he reads them as people on earth, and rejects the explanation that they are the patriarchs. Rashi and Meiri read the dead patriarchs; Radak and Metzudat David the living pious; Malbim the idols.

'Majestic, mighty ones', in construct form before 'all my delight'. Radak and Meiri discuss the construct and compare it with 'windows of closed frames' (1 Kgs 6:4) and 'plants of pleasantness' (Isa 17:10), where a construct is followed by an adjective-like noun; the sense is the same group, or a second group, in whom he delights.

verses.translation_literal: Their sorrows will multiply, [those who] hurried [after] another. I will not pour out their drink offerings of blood, and I will not lift up their names upon my lips.
verses.translation_dramatic: Their griefs will grow, and grow again, those who ran, who hurried after some other god. I will not pour their drink offerings, those red libations. I will not so much as carry their names on my lips.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the psalm changes pace, and its tone goes cold. The first clause turns on the verb 'maharu', from which comes 'mohar', the bride-price a man pays for a wife (Gen 34:12, Ex 22:15). Radak, Metzudat Zion and Meiri note this: the people may be those who 'pay a bride-price for another', that is, who buy themselves into the cult of another god, as the ASV has it ('give gifts for another god'). The KJV 'hasten after' and BBE 'go after' follow the other reading, 'hurry'. YLT's 'hastened backward' is a stretch. Keep both: the verb sounds like hurrying and like paying.

The 'drink offerings of blood' are libations, wine poured out beside the altar in all of the ancient Near East. 'Of blood' is a harsh phrase. It may mean wine mixed with sacrificial blood (Ibn Ezra), or, as Radak and Meiri have it, a prophetic exaggeration: with ill-gotten gain, with violence, the libation is blood. The KJV's 'will I not offer' hides the verb 'asikh', 'pour out'. Rashi: 'I will not be like them, to throw blood for a foreign god.'

The last line is about law as well as taste. To 'lift up a name on the lips' is to invoke it; Exodus 23:13 tells Israel not to let the names of other gods be heard from the mouth. Hosea 2:19 has the LORD say he will remove the names of the Baals. Audience: the speaker will not even say their names. The voice goes quiet and flat here: this is a boundary, not a tantrum.

'Atsvotam', 'their sorrows', is a pun on 'atsabim', idols: the same root 'atsav' means to grieve and to fashion. The sound play is audible in Hebrew.

philological_notes.note: Either 'they hurried' or, from 'mohar' (bride-price, Gen 34:12; Ex 22:15), 'they paid a bride-price / bought'. Radak, Metzudat Zion and Meiri give both; ASV 'give gifts' follows the second.
Hiphil of nasakh: to pour out a libation. 'Nesekh' is the drink offering. Metzudat Zion glosses 'asikh' as casting, throwing.
'Their sorrows'. The root 'atsav' means both to grieve and to shape; 'atsabim' are idols. The echo is in the sound. This is my own observation.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH [is] the portion of my share and of my cup; you [are] holding my lot.
verses.translation_dramatic: But the LORD, the LORD is my portion, my share, my cup. And you, you hold my lot in your hand and will not let it fall.
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood shifts from refusal to the quietest confidence in the chapter. This is landlord language. In Israel the land was divided by lot among the tribes and clans (Joshua 13-19), and the Levites alone received no plot: 'the LORD is his inheritance' (Deut 10:9, 18:2). The speaker uses the same words for what he has been given: 'portion' (menat), 'share' (cheleq), 'lot' (goral). The point is that the speaker's property is not a field but God. Compare Psalm 73:26.

The cup is the portion of drink at a meal, a host's gift to a guest, a fate (compare Ps 23:5, 'my cup runs over'). Ibn Ezra, however, takes 'kosi' as just another word for 'portion', from the verb in Exodus 12:4, and rejects 'the cup of drink'. The KJV drops 'my share and my cup' into one phrase, 'the portion of mine inheritance and of my cup', and loses the triple repetition.

'Tomikh' is odd in form. Rashi, citing the Sifrei, derives it from a sense of 'to bring low', pressing the hand down on the lot, as in Eccl 10:18, and offers 'to hold up' as the plain reading. Ibn Ezra and Radak read it as 'tamakh', to hold up, support, with an irregular vowel. KJV's 'maintainest' is archaic, but near the sense; YLT 'uphold', BBE 'supporter of my right'. Rashi and Metzudat David: like a father who takes the hand of a beloved child and places it on the best portion, saying, 'choose this one'.

philological_notes.note: 'The portion of my share': the same idea piled up. Radak says that the portion, the share, the cup and the lot are one thing said in different words to strengthen it, as the language does. In Israel's land division the Levites' 'share' was the LORD himself (Deut 10:9).
An unusual form. Rashi takes it as 'bring low, press down' (the Sifrei) with 'support' as a second sense; Ibn Ezra and Radak as 'tamakh', to uphold.

verses.translation_literal: Boundary lines have fallen for me in pleasant [places]; also an inheritance is beautiful upon me.
verses.translation_dramatic: The measuring lines have fallen for me in sweet places. Yes, the land that is mine is lovely to look on, and it sits on me like a gift.
verses.directors_commentary:
The images here come from surveying. A 'chevel' is a cord, and a cord is a measure of land: the lot falls and the line is stretched around a field, and the field is yours. Two things are packed into the one word, the rope and the plot it marks out. 'Fallen for me' is the language of the lot (compare 'goral' in the previous verse); Joshua 17:5 and 19:9 use 'chevel' for a territory. The KJV's 'The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places' is excellent English and nearly literal, a rare exception, and the same phrase has stayed in English speech ever since. The BBE's 'Fair are the places marked out for me' loses 'fall' and the lot.

'Naimim' is 'pleasant things'. The Hebrew has no word for 'places'; the translators supply it, as the word in brackets shows. Ibn Ezra says the missing noun is 'places', as in a figure of speech; Rashi and Meiri say the pleasant thing is God himself, whom the speaker drew as his lot. Metzudat David says the same: 'the God I have chosen'.

The second line says 'beautiful upon me': a gift of land that suits the one who wears it. Radak notes that men who divide land normally eye each other's shares; this speaker does not envy anyone. This is the first time we hear the ancient reader's old complaint turned over: here is a man who is happy with his draw. Keep the voice warm, not smug.

philological_notes.note: Surveyor's cords, hence the plots marked out with them, allotted portions. Ibn Ezra glosses 'portions'; Metzudat Zion 'districts', as in Josh 19:9.
Written with a final taw as if in construct, but taken by Radak as the feminine ending taw for hey (like 'ozi vezimrat Yah' in Ex 15:2): 'an inheritance', not 'the inheritance of'.

verses.translation_literal: I will bless YHWH, who has counseled me; also [in] nights my kidneys have instructed me.
verses.translation_dramatic: I will bless the LORD, who gave me counsel. And in the nights, even in the nights, when the house is still, my own kidneys, the deepest part of me, teach me.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the only place in the psalm where the blessing is said out loud. 'Avarekh' is a promise: 'I will bless', and one blesses a God who has just advised one. The second half is the surprise. The Hebrew says the speaker's 'kilyot', his kidneys, instruct him at night. In Hebrew thought the kidneys are the seat of conscience and the inner life; God 'tests the heart and kidneys' (Ps 7:10, Jer 11:20), and the Talmud's phrase quoted by Radak is that 'the kidneys give counsel, the heart understands' (Berakhot 61a). The KJV 'reins' is an old English word for kidneys, now unrecognizable. The ASV 'my heart' and the BBE 'my thoughts' soften a very physical word. Say it plainly: kidneys.

'Leilot' is the plural 'nights', not 'in the night seasons' (KJV). Ibn Ezra, Radak and Metzudat David all note that night is when a man is alone and his mind is free of the day's business. Rashi gives a midrashic reading: Abraham, who learned Torah by himself before it was given.

'Yissruni' is 'instruct, discipline'; the root 'yasar' has a school-teacher's discipline in it, not just advice. So God counsels from outside, and the body teaches from within. Play this half in a lower voice, a man who has been woken by his own conscience and does not resent it.

philological_notes.note: 'My kidneys': in Hebrew, the seat of conscience and inward feeling (compare Ps 7:10; 16:7; Jer 11:20). Radak quotes the Talmud: 'the kidneys counsel, the heart understands' (Berakhot 61a).
To instruct, discipline, correct. A teacher's or a parent's word, stronger than 'advise'.

verses.translation_literal: I have placed YHWH before me continually, for [he is] at my right hand; I will not be shaken.
verses.translation_dramatic: I have set the LORD in front of me, and I keep him there, always. He stands at my right hand, and so I will not be shaken.
verses.directors_commentary:
The picture is a bodyguard. In an ancient battle line the soldier's shield side was on the left, which left his sword arm, his right, exposed; the one who stands at the right hand is the one who protects his weak side, and a defending counsel stood there in court (Ps 109:31). So 'at my right hand' means 'he is my defender'. The KJV 'at my right hand' is correct and well-known; the actor should hear it as a protector standing beside him.

'Shiviti' is 'I have set, placed, made level', in the sense of putting something in position where you can see it; Jewish tradition has made the line famous as the opening of the 'shiviti' plaque in synagogues. The Hebrew verb is in the perfect tense: 'I have placed' a thing and left it. 'Tamid' is 'continually', every moment, not a once-off. Radak and Metzudat David say: as if God stood in front of me and saw my deeds. Radak, citing Maimonides, adds that the right hand is the one a man never forgets, because it moves so lightly.

The last word, 'emmot', is 'I will be shaken', 'I will totter'. BBE 'I will not be moved' follows the KJV. Radak glosses it simply: 'I will not fall'. The Hebrew 'bal' is the poetic 'not' used throughout this psalm.

philological_notes.note: To set, place, set level. Metzudat Zion compares 'mesavveh raglai' (Ps 18:34). The line is the source of the synagogue 'shiviti' plaque.
'From my right hand', that is, at my right. The right was the protector's side and the side of the one who helps; Radak adds, citing Maimonides, that it is the hand a man never forgets.

verses.translation_literal: Therefore my heart is glad and my glory rejoices; also my flesh will dwell in security.
verses.translation_dramatic: And so my heart is glad, and my whole soul sings out; even my body, my flesh, will lie down and live without fear.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Therefore' ties the joy to the previous verse: he is glad because the LORD stands at his side. Then the verse runs through the whole man, in three words: heart, glory, flesh. 'Libbi' is the heart, the mind and will (Ibn Ezra: 'the intellect'); 'kevodi' is 'my glory', which Ibn Ezra, Radak and Metzudat David all read as the soul, 'the glory of the body'; and 'besari' is the flesh, the plain body.

The KJV 'my flesh also shall rest in hope' is a piece of translation that quietly changes the Hebrew. 'Lavetach' means 'to security', 'in safety', 'unafraid'; the ASV and Rashi's sentence get it right. 'Hope' does not appear in the Hebrew at all. The reader who knows the later use of this psalm in the New Testament may hear 'hope' here, but that comes through the Greek of the Septuagint, not the Hebrew. Radak notes that the line has two possible senses, safe in this life, or, as the midrash he quotes, safe from worms after death (Bava Batra 17a).

The whole verse is body language. The actor should not play abstract joy: the man's chest is loose, his hands unclenched, he can finally sleep. 'Shakhan' is 'to dwell, settle', as in a tent that is pitched.

philological_notes.note: 'My glory, my honour', the soul as the glory of the body (Radak, Ibn Ezra, Metzudat David).
'To security, in safety'. It is not 'in hope' (KJV), which has no word in the Hebrew.

verses.translation_literal: For you will not leave my soul to Sheol; you will not give your faithful one to see the pit.
verses.translation_dramatic: For you will not leave me, my very life, to Sheol. You will not hand your faithful one over to look down into the pit.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the verse the psalm has been walking toward, and its two halves say the same thing in two voices: 'my soul' and 'your faithful one' are the same person. Let the second line widen the first. 'Soul' here is nefesh, the life and the self, not a ghost that leaves the body; 'my nefesh' is simply 'me'. Sheol is the underworld of the dead, the place Israel imagines under the earth, silent and cut off from praise. 'Leave to Sheol' means abandon there, give up to it.

The KJV makes two decisions that matter. 'Hell' for Sheol imports a later picture of punishment that the word does not carry; the Hebrew means the realm of all the dead. And 'corruption' for shachat has the Hebrew reading 'see the pit', with the same verb 'see' used of experiencing something. The KJV, YLT, ASV and Webster in the packet all say 'corruption'; the BBE's 'place of death' goes with 'pit'. The word can be derived either as a pit or as decay, and the tradition does not agree: Meiri takes it as Gehinnom, a place of punishment, and Radak and Metzudat David take the line as the soul not being left in the grave. The Greek version behind the New Testament quotations in Acts 2:27 and 13:35 renders it 'corruption', which is background knowledge and not part of the Hebrew evidence here.

The verb 'give' (titen) in 'will not give your faithful one' is a handing-over: God as the one who would be doing it. 'Hasid', the one bound to God by loyalty, is the KJV's 'Holy One' with capitals, which sharpens it to a title; the Hebrew has a lowercase loyal person. Speak it with calm certainty, not triumph.

philological_notes.note: Either 'pit' or 'decay, corruption', depending on whether it is derived from a root meaning to sink or one meaning to destroy. The STEPBible gloss in the packet is 'the pit'. The KJV, YLT, ASV and Webster say 'corruption'; the BBE says 'the place of death'. Meiri reads it as a place, Gehinnom. This is my own reading of the evidence and not a lexicon citation.

'My life, my self.' The word does not mean a separate immortal soul; Metzudat David and Malbim read it as the soul, but the plain sense is the person himself. Parallel with 'your faithful one' in the second line.

verses.translation_literal: You will make known to me the path of life; a fullness of joys [is] with your face; pleasant things [are] at your right hand, perpetuity.
verses.translation_dramatic: You will show me the path of life. Before your face there is fullness, a fullness of joy. At your right hand are sweet things, and they do not end.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends in a room, not on a road. 'Orach chayyim', 'the path of life', is a road image from wisdom writing: the path of the righteous leads to life (Prov 2:19, 5:6, 15:24). But the second half moves to a court, to the presence of a king. 'Et panekha' is 'with your face', 'in your presence', and a king's face is where favour is given. 'Sova' is the fullness of a good meal, being sated, and it is joined to 'semachot', joys, in the plural: not a mood, but a table of gladnesses. The KJV 'fulness of joy' is excellent.

The last line has a soft spot. 'Ne'imot' is 'pleasant things', sweetnesses, mild and warm things, not the 'pleasures' of the KJV, which sounds more sensual than the Hebrew. 'At your right hand' is the place of honour at a royal table, where gifts are given (Radak: 'the face and the right hand are honour', and he cites Ps 110:1). Ibn Ezra: 'as one who gives pleasant gifts to his beloved with his right hand'. The right hand returns from verse 8: there the LORD stands at the speaker's right as defender; here the speaker is at the LORD's right as guest.

'Netsach' is 'perpetuity, lastingness', and the KJV's 'for evermore' makes it theological. It is at least 'for good', 'without end'. The commentators (Ibn Ezra, Radak, Malbim, Metzudat David) hear the world to come; Rashi calls the verb 'future, not a prayer'. The actor does not have to choose, only to hold the doors open: the line ends with a word that does not stop.

philological_notes.note: 'The path of life', a wisdom-literature phrase (Prov 2:19; 5:6; 15:24). Radak reads it as the way by which the soul lives on after the body; Rashi calls the verb a future, not a prayer.
Fullness, satiety, the feeling after a meal that has satisfied; joined with the plural 'joys' to give 'a fullness of joys'.
Perpetuity, lastingness. Ibn Ezra: the gifts will never stop. The word is closer to 'forever' as 'without end' than to a doctrine of eternity.
